questions.question: How do you write a unit test for a Spring @Service using Mockito?
questions.title: Unit Test Spring Service Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Don't load Spring at all — use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with @Mock for the repository and @InjectMocks for the service.** This runs in milliseconds. Only use @SpringBootTest for true integration tests that need the full context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the difference between a Spring integration test and a fast unit test of a Spring service
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Loading @SpringBootTest for every service test — makes the test suite 100x slower than necessary
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete well-structured service unit test and explain why NOT loading Spring is the right choice

sections.title: Unit Test: No Spring Context Needed
Key Points
sections.content:
- @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class): no Spring, fast
- @Mock CustomerRepository: fake repository
- @InjectMocks CustomerService: REAL service with mocks injected
- Test runs in milliseconds
- @SpringBootTest: loads full context, takes seconds — don't use for unit tests
- Test the service's logic: happy path, edge cases, error handling
- Mock only external dependencies — the service itself is real
- This is the primary way to test Spring service business logic

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To unit test a Spring @Service I don't load Spring at all. I use @ExtendWith with MockitoExtension, create @Mock for the repository dependency, and @InjectMocks for the service — which creates a real CustomerService instance with the mock repository injected. In the test I stub the repository to return test data, call the service method, and assert the result. This runs in milliseconds. Using @SpringBootTest would load the entire Spring context for no benefit in a pure logic test. I only use @SpringBootTest when I'm testing that beans wire together correctly or when I need real infrastructure like a real database.

questions.title: Spring MockMvc Controller Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use `@WebMvcTest` with `MockMvc` to test the controller layer without starting a full server.** Inject the controller's dependencies with `@MockBean`. MockMvc performs HTTP requests in memory and lets you assert on status, headers, and JSON body.

sections.title: MockMvc: In-Memory HTTP Testing
Key Points
sections.content:
- @WebMvcTest: loads only web layer (Controller, ControllerAdvice)
- @MockBean: mock the service — required since real bean not loaded
- MockMvc: perform HTTP requests, chain andExpect assertions
- status().isOk(), status().isNotFound(), etc.
- jsonPath("$.field"): assert JSON response body
- content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
- perform(post().content(json).contentType(...)): for POST tests
- @WebMvcTest doesn't load @Service, @Repository — use @MockBean for them

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To test a Spring REST controller I use @WebMvcTest which loads only the web layer without starting a full server. I autowire MockMvc and use @MockBean to provide the service dependency. In the test I use mockMvc.perform with get or post and a URL, then chain andExpect calls to verify the status code, content type, and JSON response body using jsonPath expressions. This is much faster than @SpringBootTest because it only loads the MVC layer. I stub the service to return test data and focus the test on the controller's behavior: correct HTTP status codes, response serialization, and error handling.

sections.title: @DataJpaTest: Lightweight JPA Slice Test
Key Points
sections.content:
- @DataJpaTest: loads JPA, embedded H2, @Repository beans
- Does NOT load @Service, @Controller
- Each test runs in a transaction, rolled back after → no DB pollution
- TestEntityManager: for setting up test data directly

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To test a Spring Data JPA repository I use @DataJpaTest which loads only the JPA layer with an embedded H2 database. Each test runs in a transaction that's automatically rolled back after the test, so there's no database pollution between tests. I use TestEntityManager to set up test data and then call repository methods to verify they return the right results. This is the right layer to test custom JPQL queries, derived query methods, and entity constraints. I wouldn't test standard save and findById from Spring Data — those are already tested by the framework. I'd use @AutoConfigureTestDatabase with replace=NONE if I need to test against the real database dialect.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and slice test annotations?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest vs Slice Tests Spring Boot | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **@SpringBootTest loads the entire application context — all beans, all configs.** Slice tests (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@JsonTest`) load only the relevant layer. Slice tests are faster and more focused; use @SpringBootTest only for true end-to-end integration tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot testing layers — a key practical knowledge area
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for everything — slow and tests more than intended
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the slice tests, explain what each loads, and give a concrete scenario for when @SpringBootTest is appropriate

sections.title: Full Context vs Focused Layer
sections.content: **@SpringBootTest**: loads ALL beans, all auto-configurations. Use for true integration tests or verifying application context wires together. Slow. **@WebMvcTest**: only controller layer + MVC infrastructure. Use for controller tests with MockMvc. **@DataJpaTest**: only JPA + embedded DB. For repository tests. **@JsonTest**: only Jackson serialization. For DTO serialization tests. **@WebFluxTest**: reactive web layer. Choose the narrowest annotation that covers what you're testing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @SpringBootTest: full context — seconds
- @WebMvcTest: MVC layer — sub-second
- @DataJpaTest: JPA + H2 — sub-second
- @JsonTest: Jackson only — milliseconds
- @RestClientTest: rest template + mock server
- Slice tests: faster CI, more focused failures
- @SpringBootTest use cases: smoke tests, context loading tests, E2E
- Combine with @MockBean for slice tests when some beans must exist
- Context caching: same context reused across tests with same config

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @SpringBootTest loads the entire application context which includes all beans, configurations, and auto-configurations. It's slow — takes seconds — and should be reserved for true integration tests or smoke tests that verify the application starts correctly. Slice tests are the right choice for focused layer testing: @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories, @JsonTest for serialization. They load only the relevant layer, run much faster, and produce more focused test failures. I build my test pyramid with many unit tests using plain Mockito, some slice tests for each layer, and very few @SpringBootTest tests for full integration scenarios.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service that has a @Transactional method?
questions.title: Testing a @Transactional Spring Service
questions.direct_answer: For unit tests, mock the repository and test business logic without transactions; for integration tests, use @DataJpaTest with real database transactions and @Transactional rollback per test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can distinguish what unit tests should cover versus what integration tests should cover for transactional services
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to test @Transactional behavior in a unit test, which does not work because the transaction proxy is part of Spring's context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Transactional in unit tests has no effect because Spring's transaction proxy is not active without a loaded context

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The key insight is that @Transactional behavior — the actual begin and commit of a database transaction — only works when Spring's transaction proxy is active, which requires a Spring context. In a plain unit test with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), no Spring context is loaded, so @Transactional annotations on your service methods are completely ignored.

This is actually fine for unit testing because you should be mocking the repository anyway. Your unit test goal is to verify business logic: given this input, does the service call the right repository methods with the right arguments, compute the correct values, and handle exceptions properly? You test all of that by mocking the repository and injecting it with @InjectMocks. Transaction management is infrastructure, not business logic, so it belongs in integration tests.

For integration testing transactional behavior — rollback on exceptions, transaction propagation, optimistic locking — you use @DataJpaTest, which loads only the JPA layer with a real database (H2 by default) and real transactions. Each test gets its own transaction that is rolled back automatically after the test, keeping tests isolated.

If you need to test the full stack including the service, you can use @SpringBootTest with a @Transactional annotation on the test class to roll back after each test. The important thing is to be intentional: unit tests for logic, integration tests for transaction behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
content: @Transactional has no effect in unit tests — the Spring transaction proxy is not active
Unit tests: mock the repository with @Mock, test business logic only
@DataJpaTest: loads only the JPA layer, real transactions, H2 by default, rollback per test
@SpringBootTest + @Transactional on test class: full stack integration test with automatic rollback

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service method that calls an external REST API?
questions.title: Testing Services with External REST Calls
questions.direct_answer: Mock the RestTemplate or WebClient dependency with @Mock, stub its exchange/get methods with when().thenReturn(), and assert on what your service does with the response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to isolate HTTP client dependencies in unit tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting the test actually call the real external API, making it slow and flaky
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention WireMock as a better tool for integration-level HTTP testing, while Mockito suffices for unit tests

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When your Spring service depends on an HTTP client like RestTemplate or WebClient to call an external REST API, you should never let the test make real network calls. Real HTTP calls make tests slow, flaky, and environment-dependent.

For a unit test, you mock the HTTP client. If your service uses RestTemplate injected via constructor, you create a @Mock RestTemplate restTemplate and pass it to the service in @BeforeEach. Then you stub the method your service calls: when(restTemplate.getForObject(anyString(), eq(UserDto.class))).thenReturn(new UserDto("Alice", "alice@example.com")). Your test then calls the service method and asserts on the result or the behaviour based on the stubbed response.

For WebClient, which uses a reactive fluent API, the stubbing is more verbose because you need to stub the entire chain — webClient.get().uri().retrieve().bodyToMono() — which requires stubs for each builder object. Many developers extract a WebClient wrapper interface with a single fetchUser(String id) method and mock that interface instead, which is much cleaner.

For integration tests where you want to test the actual HTTP serialisation and the full client setup, use WireMock. WireMock starts a real HTTP server on localhost, you configure expected requests and canned responses, and your service hits that server. This tests the full HTTP stack without touching the real external service.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Mock RestTemplate or WebClient with @Mock and stub response methods.
For WebClient's fluent API, wrap it behind an interface for easier mocking.
Use WireMock for integration-level tests that exercise real HTTP serialisation.
Never let unit tests make real network calls — they become slow and flaky.

questions.question: How do you test exception handling in a Spring @Service — for example, when a repository throws a DataAccessException?
questions.title: Testing Exception Handling in Spring Services
questions.direct_answer: Stub the mock to throw the exception with when().thenThrow(), then use assertThrows() from JUnit 5 to assert that your service throws the expected exception or handles it correctly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to write negative-path tests that cover error handling code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only testing the happy path and leaving exception branches uncovered
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the case where the service propagates the exception and the case where it wraps/translates it into a domain exception

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Testing exception handling is just as important as testing the happy path, and Mockito makes it straightforward. You stub the mock to throw the exception and then assert on what your service does with it.

Suppose your service catches DataAccessException from a repository and wraps it in a custom ServiceException. In your test, stub the repository to throw: when(userRepository.findById(anyLong())).thenThrow(new DataAccessException("DB down") {}). Then use JUnit 5's assertThrows: ServiceException ex = assertThrows(ServiceException.class, () -> userService.getUser(1L)). You can then assert on the exception message or cause: assertEquals("Failed to retrieve user", ex.getMessage()).

For the opposite case — where the service is supposed to swallow the exception and return a default value — you stub the throw the same way, then assert that the service returns the fallback: Optional<User> result = userService.findUser(99L); assertTrue(result.isEmpty()).

A common mistake is only testing the happy path and leaving catch blocks as dead code. This means a bug in your error handling goes undetected until production. Good code coverage tools like JaCoCo flag uncovered catch blocks, which is a signal to add a negative-path test. As a fresher, mentioning that you proactively test error paths impresses interviewers because it shows production awareness.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Use when(mock.method()).thenThrow(new ExceptionType()) to simulate failures.
Use assertThrows(ExceptionType.class, () -> ...) to assert the expected exception.
Assert on both the exception type and its message or cause for precise validation.
Always write negative-path tests for catch blocks — coverage tools flag untested ones.
